judgments.title: Zen Courts Sdn Bhd v Ferrier Hodgson MH Sdn Bhd & ors
judgments.catchwords: Keywords: Appeal by the Defendant on my decision which I dismissed – Enclosure 125 and allowed the Plaintiff’s application under Enclosure 138 – pursuant to Order 33 Rule 2 of the Rules of Court 2012 – Enclosure 125 – seeks the preliminary determination of four questions concerning independent expert/witness immunity, causation, res judicata/issue estoppel and limitation – Enclosure 138 filed – seeking the preliminary determination of two questions: whether FHMH owed Zen Courts a duty of care as an independent valuer, and whether FHMH breached that duty of care – The Plaintiff is a private limited company – FHMH is a private limited company – The Plaintiff held 4,500 ordinary shares in BJD representing 30% of the shareholding in BJD, the remaining 70% shares in BJD was held by Ho Hup – The Defendant submitted its Valuation Report, opining that the indicative value – Dissatisfied with the valuation, challenging this valuation, seeking leave to cross-examine its report – the Federal Court allowed Enclosure 80 and remitted the matter to the High Court for a full valuation hearing with liberty to cross-examine and present competing expert evidence – an independent expert – Federal Court’s decision in Ng Wai Pin v Ong Yew Teik re-emphasized that witness immunity protects witnesses of fact and experts from civil liability to preserve the finality of litigation and prevent harassment – Court’s finding not a Court-appointed expert Under Order 40 of the ROC 2012 – on the court’s own motion, must have followed strictly the statutory procedures, including submitting reports directly to the Court and the Registrar – a company and not an individual, was appointed pursuant to the mutual agreement of the parties – was contractually engaged by BJD to perform a commercial valuation and where the costs of the valuation was borne by BJD in its own Valuation Report – frequently referred to itself as an ‘independent valuer’ and never as a court-appointed expert – no formal Order 40 appointment was ever made – In Jones v Kaney (supra), the Supreme Court abolished expert witness immunity previously enjoyed by expert witnesses from civil claims in contract and tort, emphasizing that there is no conflict between the duty an expert owes to the court and the duty of care they owe to their instructing client to perform their professional task with reasonable care and skill – an expert witnesses owes a duty to their client – causation – res judicata/issue estoppel and limitation – is precluded by the doctrine of issue estoppel from raising these preliminary questions – witness immunity, causation, res judicata/estoppel, and limitation – were raised and argued in detail – in its previous striking out application – the Defendant owed Zen Courts a duty of care in conducting the valuation of BJD’s shares – the Defendant breached that duty of care by failing to exercise reasonable care and skill – pleaded that all material times – owed a contractual duty – to exercise all reasonable care and skill in the determination of the fair value of the said shares and also under a duty to act fairly and impartially and was in breach of the duty of care and/or impartiality determined the value of the said shares at a value well outside the permitted or acceptable margin of error – conditions for a duty of care are plainly satisfied – Foreseeability – Proximity – standard of care expected of a professional valuer is that of a reasonably competent valuer in the same field, possessing ordinary skill and care.

judgments.title: Pendakwa Raya & ors v Julasiri Bin Akilmara
judgments.catchwords: Offence under section 39B(1)(a) of the Dangerous Drugs Act 1952 read together with section 34 of the Penal Code - Whether the trial judge should have informed at the close of the prosecution's case, that the defence was being called upon to answer a case of actual trafficking or presumed trafficking? - Overwhelming evidence proved the elements of custody, control, and knowledge - Actual possession of the impugned drugs was established - Section 180 (1) and (4) of the Criminal Procedure Code - Procedure after conclusion of case for prosecution - No statutory or legal requirement to state the presumption when calling for the defence - Formal verbal label for an evidentiary rule at the close of the prosecution's case is unnecessary - Statutory presumption of trafficking under section 37(da)(xvi) of the Dangerous Drugs Act 1952 - Section 422 of the Criminal Procedure Code - Not vitiate the conviction - No miscarriage of justice - Failure either to make or to record such a finding does not ipso facto - The law does not require a mini-judgment or detailed legal reasons at the close of the prosecution’s case

judgments.title: Santhi A/P Ganga v JANAGI A/P J VALU
judgments.catchwords: Originating Summons - to terminate the co-ownership of the subject immovable property, direct its sale, and divide the net proceeds between the Applicant and the Respondent. Termination of co-ownership - registration of title under the NLC confers merely prima facie legal title and does not automatically vest absolute beneficial ownership in equity - as one hundred percent (100%) of the beneficial ownership resided exclusively with the Deceased during his lifetime and has now devolved onto his estate, there is absolutely no legal or factual basis for the Applicant to seek the termination of the co-proprietorship or the sale of the Property under s. 145(1) & (2)(c) of the NLC Registration of non-Muslim marriages - de facto cohabitation, regardless of longevity, does not translate into a lawful marriage, nor does it generate statutory rights over matrimonial assets. Indefeasibility of title – having been obtained through misrepresentation, the Applicant’s registered interest is rendered legally infirm, and she is barred from invoking the doctrine of indefeasibility Equitable relief - he who comes to equity must come with clean hands - such powers are not exercised arbitrarily, but require a threshold of credible and sufficient material to warrant judicial intervention

judgments.title: MUHAMMAD HANIFF RAZRI BIN HASRI v Pendakwa Raya & ors
judgments.catchwords: Criminal Justice - Dangerous Drugs Act 1952, ss. 2, 37(d), 39B(1)(a) — Trafficking — Appeal against conviction — Whether statutory presumption of deemed possession under s. 37(d) can be conflated with substantive trafficking under s. 2 by "keeping and storing" without proof of an independent positive overt act beyond reasonable doubt — Presumption stacking and impermissible inversion of burden of proof — Criminal Procedure Code, s. 180(3) — Duty of trial court to amend charge to possession under s. 39A(2) where only s. 37(d) possession proved at close of prosecution case — Mid-trial mutation of case causing incurable prejudice and breach of natural justice — Evidence Act 1950, s. 54(1) — Prejudicial reception of bad character evidence (AADK document and smoking bong) — Break in chain of custody via non-contemporaneous, post-facto reconstruction of Drug Exhibit Register (POL 260) compromising identity of dangerous drugs — Non-exclusive access to ancestral premises and negative forensic nexus — Curative provisions inapplicable where foundational evidence of possession is fatally tainted — Conviction quashed and substituted conviction under s. 39A(2) refused — Accused acquitted and discharged.

judgments.title: HONG LEONG BANK BERHAD v PJ CENTRESTAGE JMB & ors
judgments.catchwords: LAND LAW: Strata titles — Common property — Car parks, basement areas, landscaped areas, rooftops, reception area and façade areas — Whether common property under BCPA 2007 — Whether developer could subsequently register common property as accessory parcels — Effect of s 45 BCPA 2007 — Whether amendments to building plans after SPAs and CCC without purchasers’ consent were unlawful — Whether registered strata titles defeasible for fraud and misrepresentation under s 340 NLC — Corporate veil — Whether developer and purchaser companies were effectively controlled by same interests — Banking security — Unregistered equitable interests over common property — Whether banks could rely on bona fide financier principle — Duty of due diligence — Whether equitable interests were void — Appeals dismissed.
